# Strict cap profiles for open covers and independent normals

This is a scoped ordinary continuous consequence of
`candidate 55fd8fec61360536`, independently
audited in `unshared historical review/context (not an accepted premise)`.
It needs no classification of equality densities or weighted stationary
sections. It asserts no mixed-integer summation principle.

## 1. Strict-cover density lemma

Let r>=1, beta>=r+1, and let f have finite positive integral M, be
positive on an open full-dimensional convex set U, and vanish outside
U. Suppose phi=f^(-1/beta) is finite positive and convex on U. Let
H_1,...,H_m be finitely many closed halfspaces, and assume the stronger
open-cover condition

    U subset union_i int(H_i).                         (1)

Write A_i=integral_(H_i) f and gamma=gamma_r. Then for every alpha>0,

    sum_i(A_i-alpha)_+ + alpha/gamma > M.               (2)

Full or zero cap masses are permitted. The strict premise alpha>0
is deliberate; for a single full cap the profile is an equality at
alpha=0.

**Proof.** Perform the exact distal truncation from the audited source.
For A_i>alpha remove the outer parallel cap of mass A_i-alpha, and
intersect all retained closed sides to form L. Each original cap has
f-mass at most alpha within L. Put

    R=sum_i(A_i-alpha)_+.

If M-R<=0, then R+alpha/gamma>M because alpha>0. Otherwise
`M_L=integral_L f >=M-R>0`.

The attained hereditary-depth theorem supplies one point

    y in U intersect int(L)

whose every containing closed halfspace has f-mass within L at least
`gamma M_L`. By (1) there is an index i for which y lies strictly
inside H_i. Let H_i^y be the parallel halfspace with boundary passing
through y and the same orientation, so H_i^y subset H_i.

This inclusion loses a strictly positive amount of mass within L.
Indeed phi is continuous on U. A sufficiently small ball about y is
contained in U intersect int(L) intersect int(H_i), and f has a
strictly positive lower bound on that ball. The open half of this
ball outside H_i^y lies in H_i minus H_i^y and has positive volume.
Consequently

    alpha >= integral_(L intersect H_i) f
          > integral_(L intersect H_i^y) f
          >= gamma M_L
          >= gamma(M-R).

Rearranging gives (2). This treats all closed-boundary conventions
exactly, since the density assigns every hyperplane zero mass. QED.

The proof only needs an attained hereditary depth point in the positive
interior of every positive-mass convex restriction, together with a
positive local density bound. Those hypotheses are supplied by the
stated inverse-power class and are not assumed for arbitrary measures.

## 2. Strict effective-dimensional inequality for independent normals

Let K be a convex body in R^D, and let j closed halfspaces cover K,
where 2<=j<=D. Suppose their j normal vectors are linearly independent.
Let their masses be A_1,...,A_j and V=vol_D(K). Then for every alpha>0,

    sum_(i=1)^j(A_i-alpha)_+ + alpha/gamma_(j-1) > V.    (3)

No positive lower bound on the A_i is required. In particular, if all
A_i>0 and a=min_i A_i, then

    sum_i A_i-V > (j-1/gamma_(j-1)) a.                 (4)

This is strictness for each fixed configuration. It is not a uniform
positive gap over all linearly independent normal families, which can
approach dependence.

**Proof for an inclusion-minimal cover.** The independent affine margin
map has full-dimensional compact image Q in R^j disjoint from the open
negative orthant. Separation gives lambda_i>=0, not all zero, with

    t=sum_i lambda_i margin_i>=0 on K.

Minimality forces every lambda_i>0, since otherwise the positive-index
caps alone would cover K. Independence makes t nonconstant. Choose
affine coordinates (v,t,y), with v in R^(j-1), in which every margin
is homogeneous linear in (v,t). The audited projective calculation
maps z=v/t and gives a finite bounded density F in R^(j-1) for which
F^(-1/j) is convex on its open positive support. Every cap
mass and V are preserved.

Write L_i(z,1) for the projective affine margins. They satisfy

    sum_i lambda_i L_i(z,1)=1                          (5)

at every z. Hence at every z at least one of these margins is strictly
positive. Their open halfspaces therefore cover the entire projective
space, not merely the positive support. The projected normals are
nonzero: a constant projected margin would make an original margin
proportional to t, contradicting independence and the strictly positive
separator involving j>=2 margins. Section 1 applies to F with r=j-1
and beta=j, proving (3).

The t=0 set is null for ordinary volume, and the open representative
of the projective support changes only null boundary values. The strict
mass gain in Section 1 occurs inside that positive support and inside
the actual retained convex set, so it cannot disappear at an unbounded
support boundary or a distal cutting plane.

**Removing minimality.** Choose an inclusion-minimal subcover of size
j'<j. If j'=1, use its elementary profile with gamma_0=1. Otherwise
apply the already proved effective-cap-count theorem to that subcover,
with constant gamma_(j'-1), since j'<=D. It yields

    sum_(i in subcover)(A_i-alpha)_+
       +alpha/gamma_(j'-1) >= V.

The sequence gamma_0,gamma_1,... is strictly decreasing. Thus replacing
its coefficient by 1/gamma_(j-1) increases the left side strictly when
alpha>0. Restoring all omitted nonnegative terms proves (3) in the
nonminimal case too. Substitution alpha=a>0 proves (4). QED.

## 3. Scope of the strictness mechanism

The key feature is the exact positive affine margin identity (5).
There is no need to assume that a depth point is a centroid or that
its active cap volumes are equal before truncation. There is also no
need to classify radial equality densities. For comparison, if the
weighted margin identity is zero and the caps meet at one point,
the open cover can fail precisely there; canonical simplex centroid
caps are the sharp example, so strictness cannot be inferred in that
case.

For ambient mixed-integer problems, this theorem may be applied inside
one measured affine fiber when its restricted normal vectors meet its
hypotheses. It provides no common point, simultaneous distal cuts, or
sum of minima across different fibers.
